summary: Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) was the second of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, one of the most prominent companions of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the man under whose caliphate the Islamic state expanded from the Arabian Peninsula into Persia, Syria, Egypt, and beyond. Known by the title al-Faruq — the one who distinguishes between truth and falsehood — he was celebrated for his justice, his administrative genius, and his directness in the service of Islam.
biography:
Umar ibn al-Khattab ibn Nufayl al-Adawi al-Qurashi was born in Makkah around 584 CE, approximately thirteen years after the Prophet ﷺ. He came from the Banu Adi clan of Quraysh, a clan respected for its role in arbitration among the Arab tribes. In the pre-Islamic period, Umar was known for his physical strength, his skills in wrestling and horse-riding, and his role as an envoy (safir) of Quraysh — a position entrusted only to men of reputation and intelligence.

Umar initially opposed Islam with great hostility, and he is recorded among the fiercest early persecutors of the Muslims in Makkah. His conversion, which occurred around 616 CE (six years after the first revelation, according to Ibn Hisham), transformed the situation of the early Muslim community. The account of his conversion is preserved in multiple narrations: he set out intending to kill the Prophet ﷺ, was informed that his own sister Fatimah and her husband Sa'id ibn Zayd had accepted Islam, confronted them, read verses from Surah Ta-Ha written on a page in their home, and was overwhelmed — proceeding directly to the Prophet ﷺ to take the shahada. (Ibn Hisham, al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Ibn Sa'd, Vol. 3)

His acceptance of Islam was public and bold. He insisted on praying openly at the Ka'bah when previous Muslims had prayed in secrecy, symbolizing a new phase of the daw'ah. The Prophet ﷺ granted him the title 'al-Faruq' — the criterion — signifying his role in distinguishing truth from falsehood.

Umar was among the small group of muhajirin who emigrated to Madinah, and he participated in virtually all of the major battles of the Prophet's era. He was present at Badr, Uhud, al-Khandaq, Khaybar, and the Conquest of Makkah. The Prophet ﷺ praised him repeatedly. He said: 'If there were to be a prophet after me, it would have been Umar ibn al-Khattab.' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi, Hadith 3686 — graded hasan sahih). He also said: 'I have looked at paradise and I saw that the majority of its people are the poor. And I looked at hell and I saw that the majority of its people are women. And I have not seen any day more similar to another than today and the day of your coming out, O Umar.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Creation)

The Prophet ﷺ married Umar's daughter Hafsah bint Umar (RA), making Umar his father-in-law. Umar also served as one of the Prophet's closest confidants in matters of state and war.

On the death of Abu Bakr in 13 AH, Umar assumed the caliphate by appointment. He would govern for ten years and three months (13–23 AH / 634–644 CE) — the longest caliphate of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs. His tenure was defined by extraordinary administrative innovations and unprecedented territorial expansion.

Among his most consequential administrative acts: he established the diwan (state register) for distributing stipends to Muslims based on seniority in Islam; organized the judicial system appointing qadis (judges) to provinces; created the institution of the shura (consultative council); established the Islamic calendar based on the Hijrah as year one (an initiative proposed in his era and credited to Ali ibn Abi Talib's suggestion for the starting date); developed the bayt al-mal (public treasury) into a systematic institution; and set strict standards for governors, including requiring them to submit inventories of their wealth upon appointment and departure to prevent corruption.

Militarily, his caliphate saw the Battle of al-Qadisiyyah (636 CE) under Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, which broke Sassanid Persian power; the Battle of al-Yarmuk (636 CE) under Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, which opened Syria; and the conquest of Jerusalem, which Umar himself visited to receive the city's surrender from Patriarch Sophronius. His entry into Jerusalem — riding a camel, dressed simply, alternating with his servant in riding — became a celebrated image of Islamic justice. He also guaranteed the safety and rights of the Christian and Jewish inhabitants of the city in the Covenant of Umar.

Umar was also known for his personal asceticism. He wore patched clothing, carried his own water, and ate simple food despite governing an empire stretching from Persia to Egypt. He walked his markets at night to check prices. He was reported to have said: 'If a mule stumbles on the banks of the Euphrates, I fear I will be asked about it on the Day of Judgment.' (al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Ibn Sa'd; also in various narrations in al-Dhahabi's Siyar)

He was assassinated in 23 AH (644 CE) by Abu Lu'lu'ah al-Majusi (also known as Piruz al-Nahawandi), a Persian slave, while leading the Fajr prayer in Madinah. He was struck with a poisoned dagger and died three days later. He was buried next to the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr (RA) in the chamber of Aisha in Madinah. Before dying, he appointed a six-person consultative council (shura) to elect the next caliph, deliberately not naming a successor himself to preserve the consultative principle.

Classical scholars are unanimous in ranking Umar second only to Abu Bakr among the Sahaba. Ibn Kathir, al-Dhahabi, and Ibn Sa'd each devote extensive chapters to his virtues and governance. The Prophet's statement — recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari — that 'the people after me should follow Abu Bakr and Umar' encapsulates the classical Sunni view of his station.

key_events.event: Accepted Islam — transformed the public posture of the early Muslim community
Fought in the Battle of Badr
Fought in the Battle of Uhud
Participated in the Battle of al-Khandaq (the Trench)
Became second Caliph following Abu Bakr's appointment
Battle of al-Qadisiyyah — defeat of Sassanid Persian forces
Battle of al-Yarmuk — Byzantine forces defeated; Syria opened
Entered Jerusalem; received its surrender; issued the Covenant of Umar
Established the Islamic Hijri calendar (proposed starting date from Ali ibn Abi Talib)
Conquest of Egypt under Amr ibn al-As
Assassinated during Fajr prayer in Madinah; died three days later

notable_traits: Justice — held himself and his governors to the highest standard of accountability
Physical courage and directness in speech
Administrative genius — innovated state institutions still referenced in Islamic governance
Deep knowledge of Quran and Sunnah — many of his legal judgments were later confirmed by revelation
Personal asceticism despite governing an empire
